questions.q: Put the six design parts in a good order.
questions.why: Start with the decision, then data, models, evaluation, serving and monitoring.

questions.q: A chain has 1,500 stores and 800 products per store. How many series is that? (number)
Scenario: the interviewer says the forecast drives nightly store orders for fresh food. Which forecast type fits best?
options: Quantile forecasts tuned to over- and under-stock costs
why: Correct: the order quantity should come from a quantile that matches the cost ratio.
The horizon is days, not a year.

questions.q: Which is a good fallback if today's features are late?
options: Serve last week's forecast or seasonal naive
why: Correct: a simple known-good forecast keeps the system running.
Retraining does not fix late data.

questions.q: Why can zero sales be misleading in a retail data set?
options: An empty shelf shows zero sales even when demand existed (censored demand)

questions.q: Which statement best shows a trade-off?
options: A nightly batch is simple and cheap, but cannot react to changes within the day.
why: Correct: it names a benefit, a cost and the situation.

questions.q: A backtest shows a 20% lift but the A/B test shows none. What is a likely reason?
options: The metric in the backtest was not linked to the business outcome, or the roll-out differs from the backtest
The backtest was too short for sure
The A/B test is always wrong
why: Correct: forecast error is a proxy; the decision rule and operations also matter.
Possible, but the first thing to check is the link between metric and outcome.
A/B tests are the stronger evidence, though they can be noisy.
